name: Baltic Brick (1350–1450)
source_notes: Malbork Castle (Marienburg, refounded 1274 and greatly expanded after 1309): the High Castle, Middle Castle and Palace of the Grand Masters are built of coursed red brick over stone footings, with tall crow-stepped gables and pitched tile roofs rather than the low battered curtains of the Welsh castles.

Gniew Castle (begun c. 1290, rebuilt through the 14th and 15th centuries) and Lidzbark Warmiński (1350–1401): brick fortresses with corner towers, a strongly defended gatehouse and flanking drums roughly 22–38 m apart, close enough for bowshot to cover the whole curtain.

Kwidzyn Castle (1345–1390) and the Malbork Palace of the Grand Masters (c. 1390s): brick castles combine a great hall, chapel and kitchen ranges around a courtyard, with steep pitched roofs of clay tile or slate and tall gabled ends closing the domestic buildings.

Baltic brick walls of 1350–1450 are laid in tall, relatively thin courses over a pronounced plinth and a modest batter; hall and chapel roofs are carried on timber trusses, which in practice limits an unsupported range to roughly 16 m across before an aisle or vault is needed.
